verdict: Second read confirms the first reader's overall judgment: clean, close to finished, no forbidden words, no em-dashes, no exclamation points, one semicolon outside quotation. Three of eight findings survive. The essay's thesis (no explanation, but a promise and a presence) does recur as a 'doesn't X. It Y.' two-beat, but most instances are doing exegetical or pastoral work; only the mid-paragraph one in the Natural Evil section is surplus.

keep.quote: The Bible doesn't look at earthquakes and parasites and call the world finished. It calls the present order subjected and bound, in labor and waiting.
keep.tell: 'Doesn't X. It Y.' antithesis as habit: second of two in one short section (the section closes 'Rowe's fawn gets no explanation in this life. What Scripture supplies is a promise'), and the same two-beat denial runs in the Job, Romans 8:28, widow, Psalms and resurrection passages.
keep.replacement: The Bible looks at earthquakes and parasites and calls the present order subjected and bound, in labor and waiting.

keep.quote: His argument was that God cannot make creatures truly free and also guarantee what they will choose, a view of freedom many Christians in the Reformed tradition reject.
keep.tell: Bolted-on qualifying clause; a safeguard stapled to the end of a summary reads as committee voice, not a person talking.
keep.replacement: His argument was that God cannot make creatures truly free and also guarantee what they will choose. It's a view of freedom many Christians in the Reformed tradition reject.

keep.quote: The Bible saw all of this long before Lisbon.
keep.tell: Vague framing sentence and mild overclaim: 'all of this' gestures at five paragraphs of philosophy, and the skeptic hears a boast just before the essay admits Job 'doesn't answer Rowe'.
keep.replacement: The Bible took up this question long before Lisbon.

dropped: Widow at the graveside ('the doctrine was never an explanation to hand a widow at the graveside. It's a promise she may lean on later'): this is the hinge of the section and the denial half carries the one concrete image; the replacement flattened it.
'These aren't failed prayers.' (consider): a short pastoral verdict a reader in grief needs said outright; the replacement loses it.
'and they carry real weight' (consider): a plain concession in his own manner ('Some of that is true'), not method showing.

'the psalms give you permission' (consider): permission is the paragraph's deliberate thread ('before you're allowed to pray', later 'He was allowed to ask, though, and so are you'); the one semicolon is permitted.
'Baptists, my own tradition': not a tell; the brief allows it and it works as fairness, not credential. Moved to for_james.
for_james: The essay has no moment only you could have written. One real memory of your own (a hospital room, a funeral, something said too early) near 'Most of us who have stood with a grieving family' or 'We make that mistake of timing all the time' would lift the voice score. Nobody should write it for you.
'Baptists, my own tradition' names your denomination. The brief allows it; your call whether it stays.
'the father who walks out' sits in the list of human-caused suffering. It works unnamed; say if you want it gone or in the first person.
Final line, 'The hands that will wipe away every tear still carry the marks of the nails.': the most literary sentence in the piece. I think it is earned; read it aloud and decide.
